items.title: System Prompt Compression with Behavioral Verification using Eidos
items.abstract_or_text: If the language people write and the language a language model has learned share the same eidos, then a short sentence might carry a long intent without the long explanation that usually accompanies it. We take this question as our starting point and separate the sentences of a system policy from the behavioral relations those sentences are meant to preserve. We register the behavioral requirements of an original policy as atoms and link each atom to a short execution clause and to an evaluation test, a procedure we call Operational Eidos, so that input reduction and behavioral adherence can be observed separately. We reanalyzed 1,296 existing executions from six language models and generated 2,960 responses on two separate language models across length-controlled, clause-removal, policy-extension and requirement-mutation experiments, for 4,256 responses in total. Compressed representations reduced mean total input by 74.18–89.51% relative to the original policy, and in the length-controlled comparison the paired adherence difference was +0.33 percentage points, close to the original (95% interval 0.00–1.00). The shortest candidate nonetheless adhered less well than a mid-length one, and in the clause-removal and mutation experiments the direction of an effect could reverse with the handling of ambiguous judgments, while some responses omitted a newly added requirement. Short representations did carry the selected behavioral requirements, but that conclusion was available only by linking the original requirements to the actual responses, not by reading the length of the text.
